claims.text: High configurational entropy is the key factor preserving the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles at high temperatures.
Entropy stabilization minimizes atomic diffusion in near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Entropy stabilization minimizes elemental segregation and preserves a uniform solid solution during service.
Rapid quenching produces a homogeneously mixed atomic distribution at room temperature.
Mild post-synthesis high-temperature annealing promotes partial atomic diffusion and elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching locks in high configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy creates a large free-energy barrier against atomic rearrangements leading to phase separation.
Annealing increases atomic mobility, reduces the entropy advantage, and enables diffusion-driven segregation and coarsening.
Microstructural evolution affects retention of catalytic active sites.
Microstructural evolution affects retention of thermoelectric conduction pathways.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation than annealed nanoparticles after service exposure.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will coarsen more slowly than annealed nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will preserve catalytic performance better than annealed nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will preserve thermoelectric performance better than annealed nanoparticles.
At temperatures well above the stated service ranges, high configurational entropy may no longer prevent phase separation.
Particle-size distributions and non-equiatomic compositions may fall outside the proposed entropy-stabilization mechanism.
